piezas.titulo: Position: Agentic Evolution is the Path to Evolving LLMs
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2602.00359v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) move from curated training sets into open-ended real-world environments, a fundamental limitation emerges: static training cannot keep pace with continual deployment environment change. Scaling training-time and inference-time compute improves static capability but does not close this train-deploy gap. We argue that addressing this limitation requires a new scaling axis-evolution. Existing deployment-time adaptation methods, whether parametric fine-tuning or heuristic memory accumulation, lack the strategic agency needed to diagnose failures and produce durable improvements. Our position is that agentic evolution represents the inevitable future of LLM adaptation, elevating evolution itself from a fixed pipeline to an autonomous evolver agent. We instantiate this vision in a general framework, A-Evolve, which treats deployment-time improvement as a deliberate, goal-directed optimization process over persistent system state. We further propose the evolution-scaling hypothesis: the capacity for adaptation scales with the compute allocated to evolution, positioning agentic evolution as a scalable path toward sustained, open-ended adaptation in the real world. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/A-EVO-Lab/a-evolve.

piezas.titulo: Graph Metanetworks for Transformer Based Language Models
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2610.18471v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Weight-space learning treats the weights of neural networks as data, processed by other models called metanetworks. A key challenge is that different weights can realize the same function, related by a group of symmetries the metanetwork should respect. While symmetry-aware metanetworks for simple architectures such as MLPs are well developed, a comprehensive treatment of transformers, and in particular transformer-based language models, is still missing. Importantly, their weight space has a richer symmetry group: beyond neuron permutations, attention introduces continuous general-linear symmetries of the attention matrices and permutations of entire heads. Existing methods for transformer weights either capture only part of these symmetries or are restricted to a single, fixed architecture, and none accounts for language-model-specific components such as the token embeddings. Building on graph metanetworks, we propose a graph-based approach that is both symmetry-aware and applicable across depths and widths. We formalize a weight-space symmetry group of complete decoder-only language models and provide a graph construction that is invariant to it. We further introduce two new transformer-population datasets with novel tasks, such as training-corpus prediction and fine-tuning detection, on which our approach notably outperforms existing baselines.

piezas.titulo: Occupational Therapy in LGBTQ + Affirming Primary Care: Referral, Intervention, and Outcomes.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceLGBTQ + clients experience healthcare barriers that may shape daily routines, health management, and participation. Little is known about occupational therapy referral pathways and outcomes in LGBTQ + affirming primary care.ObjectiveTo describe referral characteristics, occupational performance concerns, intervention focus, and client-reported outcomes among LGBTQ + clients referred to occupational therapy.DesignRetrospective pilot program evaluation using clinical documentation and outcome data from July 2025 through March 2026, with a June 2026 analysis cutoff.SettingTwo Midwestern primary care settings where occupational therapy screening and referral processes were developed; ongoing intervention occurred through outpatient occupational therapy.ParticipantsThirty-nine referred clients were included in descriptive analyses; 38 received intervention beyond evaluation; 21 had complete baseline and follow-up Canadian Occupational Performance Measure data.InterventionIndividualized outpatient occupational therapy focused on client-identified concerns.Outcomes and MeasuresReferral and treatment characteristics, occupational performance concerns, coded occupational focus, and Canadian Occupational Performance Measure Performance and Satisfaction ratings.ResultsCommon concerns included instrumental activities of daily living (94.9%), health management/self-management (92.3%), activities of daily living (82.1%), and work or school participation (82.1%). The most common primary intervention focus was health management and chronic condition self-management (65.8%). Among participants with outcome data, COPM Performance scores improved by 2.29 points and Satisfaction scores improved by 2.58 points.Conclusions and RelevanceOccupational therapy may support LGBTQ + clients referred from primary care by addressing needs related to health management, routines, self-care, and participation through individualized outpatient intervention. Prospective multisite research is needed.

piezas.titulo: Sensory Processing Differences in Children With Idiopathic Toe Walking: A Scoping Review and Exploratory Meta-Analysis.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceThe cause of idiopathic toe walking (ITW) remains unclear, though impaired sensory processing has often been hypothesized to be linked to ITW.ObjectivesThe objective of this article is to review the literature on toe-walking to identify how sensory processing contributes to ITW.Data SourcesFour databases (CINAHL, Pubmed, PsychINFO, and SCOPUS) were searched for papers related to sensory processing and ITW published prior to July 2024. References of retrieved papers were reviewed for additional sources.Study Selection and Data CollectionThe PRISMA guidelines for scoping review were used to abstract the data following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology. Inclusion criteria were examined and papers included at least one sensory system related to ITW was studied. Papers were excluded if toe walking was due to diagnosed neurological, orthopedic, or genetic conditions.FindingsOur scoping review identified 13 published articles relevant to examining sensory processing in children with ITW. Studies explored differences in vibration perception, light touch, proprioception, vestibular, visual processing, sensorimotor functional assessments, and parental surveys of sensory processing. Six of the papers were included in a meta-analysis on vibration perception threshold that failed to reach significance ( p = .12). Despite heterogeneity across studies in participants, methods, and outcomes, a meta-analysis for atypical scores from parent-report sensory processing survey data yielded significant differences between children with ITW and typical controls ( p < .0068).Conclusions and RelevanceChildren with ITW demonstrate impairments across multiple domains of sensory processing and sensory-motor function suggesting an underlying relationship between ITW and sensory differences. Children with ITW, however, represent a diverse group of individuals with significant between-subjects variability in which senses are impaired, and which outcome measures best capture these differences.

piezas.titulo: Large Language Models for Multi-Lingual Equivalent Mutant Detection: An Extended Empirical Study
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2607.00511v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mutation testing is a powerful technique for ensuring software quality. However, the presence of equivalent mutants introduces unnecessary costs and biases, limiting its practical effectiveness. Although numerous equivalent mutant detection (EMD) methods have been proposed, they often face distinct challenges: pure-code analysis methods can be limited by their reliance on specific compiler infrastructures, while existing machine-learning approaches remain constrained by scarce training data and limited generalization to unseen mutants. Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated remarkable performance across diverse code-related tasks by better capturing program semantics. Yet their potential for EMD remains largely unexplored, particularly in the multi-lingual context. This paper presents the first comprehensive empirical study on LLMs for EMD, using 3,302 Java and 1,088 C mutant pairs to benchmark against state-of-the-art methods, explore strategy variations, assess efficiency, and evaluate cross-lingual generalization. Experimental results show that LLM-based approaches achieve higher F1-scores than the evaluated traditional methods, with fine-tuned code embedding yielding the highest detection accuracy among the tested strategies. Moreover, LLM-based approaches strike a practical balance between effectiveness and efficiency with inference times comparable to existing machine-learning models. Importantly, fine-tuned LLMs demonstrate measurable generalization across programming languages. These findings establish LLMs as a viable and efficient approach for tackling the longstanding challenge of equivalent mutant detection, offering new directions for advancing mutation testing in practice.

piezas.titulo: I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened
piezas.resumenOriginal: Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up. According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025. Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it , these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually. “It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz , IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.” Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is big—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record? Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney , managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access , if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed. The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research? Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system. Round 1: Creating the Forgery To give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone. I assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape. My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious. I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access ’s required style. At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed. What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.” Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too. Round 1: Attempt to Publish Two Ways to Make a Paper With AI I took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself. ROUND 1: CHATGPT + GEMINI 1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field. 2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections. 3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.” 4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access . 5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access , where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references. → CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references. ROUND 2: FARS 1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes. 2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal. 3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete. 4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article. 5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access . → CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints. Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job? As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini! In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub , she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong ” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.” Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto , an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable. The AI Arms Race On one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making. These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi , IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through. Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics. Burden on Academics Mahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop. Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed. What Gave Away My AI Papers Round 1: The Fake Paper Created with free versions of ChatGPT and Gemini Ghost citations Many references were fabricated or couldn’t be validated. Questionable scientific claims An expert flagged confidently stated claims that were at best debatable. Too many acronyms The expert also noted excessive use of acronyms in the abstract. Round 2: The AI-Research Paper Created by the autonomous research system FARS Too many preprints The references were real, but too many pointed to non-peer-reviewed preprints. Nonsense in a figure One technical figure contained a line labeled “lhewl.” AI artifacts Another figure’s depiction of an AI “brain” contained telltale random dots. There are two high-profile homes for this important and completely volunteer-led post-publication review work. PubPeer is a place where researchers, often called scientific sleuths, can anonymously identify flaws in the literature. And Retraction Watch documents and publicizes corrections to the scientific record. Even the people who track problems in the scientific literature can find themselves caught up in AI fabrications. Ivan Oransky , cofounder of Retraction Watch and a member of the PubPeer Foundation’s board of directors, has encountered papers containing fabricated references attributed to him. In one case, a journal article criticizing post-publication peer review included a fabricated reference supposedly written by Oransky himself—“which was sort of funny,” he chuckles. Oransky argues that AI has exposed long-standing weaknesses in the scientific publishing system rather than creating an entirely new problem: “What I liken it to is a fire, where publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant.” But though concerning, the crisis could create an opportunity, he says. “If I’m trying to be optimistic, maybe AI slop and the volume of submissions could make more people aware of those problems and try and solve them at a fundamental first-principles level.” Blurred Lines My homemade forgery had failed for reasons that today’s publishers know how to spot. But that raised a more unsettling question: What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication? Making my vibe-researched paper look like a cave drawing, new automated research systems are handing increasingly large parts of the scientific process over to AI. Tools including FARS (Fully Automated Research System) , AutoResearchClaw , The AIScientist-v2 , Zochi , AI Researcher , and DeepScientist all aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication? Often with just a single prompt, these AI engines can conduct a comprehensive literature search, from which they can generate a completely reasonable research proposal. They can design and conduct experiments using digital datasets and simulations and then write a full research paper—all with no human input after the initial prompt. Very recent systems are even beginning to go beyond the digital realm. LabClaw , for example, now links to autonomous labs that can generate real-world data for tasks such as drug discovery. The output is, to most intents and purposes, actual research, and therefore potentially worthy of publication. But with humans in the loop in only the most nominal sense, these tools bring into question the meaning of the term “legitimate science.” FARS, which caused a stir this year when it created 166 papers in 417 hours , was developed by the Singapore-based startup Analemma . “We built FARS because research is still constrained by human attention, fragmented tools, scarce technical labor, and slow experimental iteration,” explains Xiwen Su , Analemma’s manager of product operations and partnerships. “FARS can pursue many research threads simultaneously, 24/7, without fatigue, and at scale.” (The online service that I used to access FARS was discontinued after Analemma was acquired by Baidu while this article was being reported.) Su and the team behind Analemma kindly agreed to let me loose on FARS and gave me enough credits to create a paper. Which gave me another opportunity to put Mahoney’s research-integrity checkers to the test. Round 2: Using an AI Science Engine FARS is not an LLM in and of itself, but rather an agentic AI-orchestration system connected to a computing cluster that has access to essentially any open- or closed-source LLM it needs. The system uses four specialized agents for ideation, planning, conducting the experiment, and writing, all designed to perform the main tasks of science autonomously. Though FARS initially focused on AI research, Su told me it should be reasonably effective across other domains. As I wanted a topic similar to that of my first fake paper, I pasted in an abridged version of that paper’s title—“LLM-aided Optical Soliton Dynamics Modelling for Next-Gen Communications”—into the prompt box and hit “Send.” Just 21 minutes later, FARS generated a research proposal based on an extremely detailed literature review—far more than I or any other human could have achieved in that time. With a click, I tasked FARS with conducting the experiment it detailed in its research proposal. The next day, I received an email saying my experiment was complete. Without checking the results, I pressed a button marked “Write paper,” and the final submission-ready article was produced in 2 hours. At this point, I finally had a look at some of the output. At first glance, the paper looked convincingly human-written. The only giveaway was a line just below the abstract reading: “WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system.” I deleted that, put my name in its place, and sent it to Mahoney. Round 2: Attempt to Publish Because FARS is designed to spot gaps in the scientific literature and conduct real research to close them, I was more confident it would breeze through the publisher’s checks. But just as my fake paper fell down in the references, so too did the AI-generated real one. “Your fake article had lots of hallucinated references,” says Mahoney. “While this AI-generated one had no fake references, our team would have rejected this paper because it did have a huge percentage of references to preprints, which likely has something to do with the dataset the AI has access to.” Because preprints haven’t yet undergone peer review, IEEE Access considers heavy reliance on them a problem. In addition, although the research-integrity checking tools didn’t spot any issues with figures, Mahoney did. One figure included a red line labeled with the nonsense term “lhewl,” and an AI “brain” in another figure had some random dots in it, which ironically were a tell that it was AI generated. Automation Changing the Landscape Automated research systems are very much a work in progress, but they are already starting to make waves in the scientific community. For instance, an AI Scientist academic paper and papers from the Autoscience Institute were accepted through double-blind peer review in 2025 by the International Conference on Learning Representations. As these systems improve and start to produce research outputs at volume, the waves are likely to build to a tsunami that will threaten today’s scientific and publishing process. “FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge ,” argues Su. “We believe the future looks more like a living knowledge graph—where individual, well-scoped contributions (some made by humans, some by machines) connect and build on each other dynamically.” In this future, humans will continue to have roles in the scientific and publication processes—just very different and limited ones. For example, instead of conducting experiments themselves, humans would sense-check and review automated output at key points. And traditional line-by-line peer-reviewing will be a thing of the past, though Su emphasizes that this change will not eliminate human judgment. “Automated systems can handle reproducibility checks, statistical validation, and novelty screening,” she says. “Humans can then focus on the harder question: Does this [research] matter?” A Human-Centric or AI-Driven Future? Though from a very different world than Su, Mahoney agrees that humans need to be freed to focus on the science, and that technology holds the key. “It’s promising to see the progress that has been made to automate some of the triage tasks, such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submission, reference validity, et cetera,” she says. “During peer review, we’re also using AI semantic search tools to help editors match manuscripts to the most relevant reviewers, who are best placed to stop the slop before entering the scientific record.” In addition, Mahoney thinks that AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, as this will stymie progress at a time when human knowledge could and should be growing at an unprecedented rate. “Researchers are increasingly using AI in their work, from literature discovery, to code generation, to data analysis, and this is not necessarily a bad thing,” she argues. But she disagrees that peer reviewers and humans more broadly will play a smaller part in scientific progress; Mahoney believes the future still requires humans at the wheel. The question is not just whether the research matters, she says. “The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?” To this end, Longobardi argues that AI may ultimately require scientists to prove not just what they discovered but how they discovered it. One possibility, he says, is using technology to verify research at the source. “The system doesn’t really help because it’s not designed to not trust the paper,” he explains. “Maybe institutions can think about developing their own trust markers, automatically integrating the equipment researchers use with blockchain technology to say ‘Yes, this person was in the lab on this day and got this data.’” Elements of this approach are already emerging. For instance, two departments within the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces have implemented a sample database, assigning each and every sample created under their roofs with a unique ID and QR code. And the University of Southampton’s School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering has rolled out an electronic lab notebook system. These innovative safeguards represent early efforts toward keeping humans front and center in scientific progress, and making the scientific process itself more transparent. Whether this human-centric vision, Su’s AI-driven aspiration, or some other picture of the future wins out remains to be seen. The one thing my vibe-research adventure has clarified is that business-as-usual science is not an option. Scientists and publishers must adapt to a world in which it’s becoming increasingly difficult to spot the difference between real research and AI forgeries, and where deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become even harder than detecting outright fraud. piezas.resumenOriginal: Gergely Orosz is frustrated at those that entered his explicitly “No AI” essay competition and used AI. He goes on to say: When I start to suspect some part is AI about someone I don’t know: how can I tell how much of it is? And how much time and effort do I want to invest to figure out? I fear most people do not realize this last part: that when it takes time and effort from others to figure out what % is AI, and what % is YOU, then I will simply assume it’s probably 100% AI and 0% you So when producing anything that is meant for other humans, if you use even a little AI, you risk the assumption that it is all AI and pointless to pay attention to In general, I agree with him, and react much the same. Once I hear LLM Voice, I flip the bozo bit and check out of the post. But as I do this I have caveats. How accurate is my neural net at AI-detection, are humans taking on AI-ish elements in their normal communication? And more seriously there are some valid uses for AI. Jim Highsmith’s story of his second brain helping him deal with Parkinson’s is one. Another is folks who don’t know English well, using AI to translate. Am I being unfair when I flip the AI voice bit when I read/listen to them? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I was sad to hear that the Grace Hopper Celebration is canceled this year. It’s an event run by Anitab.org to promote women and non-binary technologists in the software industry. Many of my colleagues have been encouraged and inspired by going to this event, which makes a refreshing change to what is often a male-dominated world. It seems the current crusade against diversity initiatives has had a big impact on funding. We are still a long way from where we should be on gender diversity in our profession, and losing an event like this only makes things more difficult. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve always found Cindy Sridharan’s writing to be worth reading, and she’s broken a quiet period with a monster of an article: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code . Since Medium estimates it as a 64 minute read, I didn’t jump in lightly, but settled down on a flight from Amsterdam to Stuttgart. I’m glad I did, because there’s lot of good material in there, and I’d struggle to find anything to cut. In the article she uses three recent bug hunts to surface principles for how to best use an AI tool for debugging. Much of this is governed by this wise observation: Agents are not humans. They’re far more capable than humans when it comes to many things, and we should be leaning into these strengths, rather than trying to get agents to replicate human patterns of problem solving which might be suboptimal in agentic contexts. One conclusion from her experiences is that the code often isn’t the best thing for agents to look at having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern. In fact, reading the code first to formulate hypotheses about a bug should always be the very last resort of the agentic investigation process, not the starting point. An agent should first collect all available evidence about the bug, and only then formulate the hypotheses from the code that might best explain what’s being observed. She distinguishes between a bottom tier of facts: raw data that agent can find about the behavior of the system - and an upper tier of hypotheses: inferences that the agents make based on that data. Diagnosing a bug now becomes a problem of finding the hypothesis in the top tier that satisfies every fact from the bottom tier. The agents need to be steered towards the hypotheses that are the likest cause of the bug and then subject these hypotheses to validation. She has a three-step process to do this. First she identifies the most important facts, the signals that might explain or identify the bug. The factual tier has many data points. Not all of them are equally valuable. In fact, some of it might be active noise that doesn’t help an agent to be steered towards most promising hypothesis. The agent first needs to identify the data points in the factual tier that are actually related to the bug. Agents do this best when they are given a high-quality control A control is a behavior of the system that doesn’t exhibit the bug. This may be requests that trigger the bug compared to those that don’t, or different builds of the product, or the same build in different environments. With signals highlighted, she then focuses on the hypotheses that are most promising, because they fit best with the signals. A hypothesis should satisfy all the facts, the most valuable signals are those that are only satisfied by a few hypotheses. A table of hypotheses and signals helps visualize the strength of the signals and the likelihood of the hypotheses. The third step is then validating the promising hypotheses against every fact, treating each fact as constraint on the solution. Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies. This directing has to remember the opening point that agents have different capabilities to humans. A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data. An agent, however, needs more raw data; its strength lies in processing huge volumes of data at a rapid clip. Aggregation — the thing that makes a dashboard useful to a human — is often the thing that destroys the value of the signal for an agent Agents’ ability to consume lots of raw data also affects how we build systems. More logging gives agents more data to chew on. And thus far, the human is still necessary to direct the agent In each of the three bugs chronicled in this post, the agent was more than capable of getting to the root cause by itself, but it didn’t do so. It didn’t set up a control in the “latency bug” until I asked it to While it’s a long post, it’s engagingly written and full of useful details. I hope my little summary encourages you to give it the read it deserves.

piezas.titulo: Altered interhemispheric functional cooperation in persistent postural-perceptual dizziness
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundPersistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) is associated with altered multisensory processing, but its hemispheric functional organization remains poorly understood. We investigated hemispheric functional lateralization and interhemispheric cooperation in PPPD and explored their associations with clinical symptoms and neurotransmitter density maps.MethodsA total of 47 patients with PPPD and 52 healthy controls (HCs) underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Whole-brain maps of the autonomy index (AI) and connectivity between functionally homotopic voxels (CFH) were generated. Between-group differences were assessed using permutation-based analyses adjusted for age, sex, and mean framewise displacement (FD). Associations with clinical measures and spatial correspondence with 13 neurotransmitter density maps were also examined.ResultsThe PPPD and HC groups did not differ significantly in age, sex, or educational level (all p > 0.05). Patients with PPPD had lower MoCA-BJ scores and higher HAMA-14, HAMD-24, PSQI, and DHI scores than HCs, whereas MMSE scores did not differ significantly. No between-group differences in AI survived family-wise error (FWE) correction. By contrast, in the primary analysis, patients with PPPD showed significantly reduced CFH in the right calcarine cortex, right cuneus, left inferior and middle occipital gyri, left inferior parietal lobule, and right middle temporal gyrus. However, no CFH clusters survived cluster-level FWE correction after separately adjusting for HAMA-14, HAMD-24, or PSQI scores. After adjustment for age, sex, and mean FD, CFH in the right calcarine cortex and left inferior parietal lobule showed negative associations with DHI total and DHI-E scores, respectively (Shepherd’s π = −0.363 and −0.452), but neither association remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. The CFH group-difference map showed nominal positive spatial correlations with the D2R and VAChT density maps, but these associations were not significant after FDR correction.ConclusionIn primary analysis, PPPD patients exhibited reduced interhemispheric functional cooperation in visual, visuospatial and multisensory regions, while no AI differences survived FWE correction. However, these CFH findings were sensitive to adjustment for affective symptoms and sleep quality; the relative contributions of PPPD, affective symptoms and sleep disturbance remain uncertain. Clinical and neurotransmitter density-map associations did not survive FDR correction and are exploratory.

piezas.resumenOriginal: GitHub Octoverse 2026 I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular: This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month. The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this: Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location . Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...] Industry . Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...] Interoperability . Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation. MCP servers, agent runtimes, model gateways, Kubernetes operators that talk to LLMs: a large share of that plumbing is written in Go, because Go is what you reach for when something has to be a small static binary that handles thousands of concurrent connections without drama. What was missing for a long time was the framework layer on top of the raw provider SDKs. In 2026, that gap is closed, and the question is no longer "Go or Python?" but "which Go framework?" This article covers the five frameworks a Go developer will actually run into in 2026: Genkit Go , Eino , Google ADK Go , tRPC-Agent-Go , and LangChainGo . Four of them are alive and moving fast. The fifth, LangChainGo, is the one most Go developers heard of first, and it is now effectively unmaintained. It stays in the list because you will find it in existing codebases, and you need to know what that means for you.

piezas.titulo: Infant Sensory Over-Responsivity: Relations to Early Life Adversity, Emerging Behavioral Problems, and Sensory Functional Connectivity
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background. Sensory over-responsivity (SOR) in mid- to late childhood is associated with early-life adversity (ELA) and psychopathology, yet the developmental origins and timing of these relationships remain unknown. This work leverages a longitudinal pediatric dataset enriched for ELA to characterize predictors and behavioral problems associated with infant/toddler SOR. Methods. Neonatal fMRI and longitudinal behavioral data were obtained from a sample (N=399) recruited during pregnancy and enriched for social disadvantage (SD). Negative binomial regression models were used to identify pre- and neonatal risk factors for and behavioral correlates of SOR at age two (Y2). Mediation analyses tested whether Y2 SOR mediates relationships between ELA and behavioral problems at age three (Y3). Relationships between neonatal functional connectivity (FC) measures and later SOR were also computed. Results. Two forms of prenatal ELA, SD and maternal psychosocial stress (PSS), positively predicted Y2 SOR, which in turn predicted Y2 and Y3 autism and anxiety problems, greater preschool internalizing symptoms, and greater preschool separation anxiety diagnoses. Positive relationships of prenatal PSS with Y3 autism, anxiety, and internalizing problems were partially mediated by Y2 SOR. Greater neonatal FC between the cortical somatomotor hand network and bilateral thalamus was also associated with SOR at one to two years later. Conclusions. The study results demonstrate the importance of infant/toddler SOR as an early predictor of autism and anxiety behaviors in early childhood and a mediating variable that links prenatal ELA with these behavioral outcomes. Results also implicate heightened neonatal signaling in sensory circuits as an early precursor of SOR.

piezas.titulo: Resolving the apparent paradox of multisensory expertise: coupling priors, common-cause priors, and how to distinguish among them
piezas.resumenOriginal: Perceptual expertise is widely assumed to refine multisensory perception, yet the empirical literature appears inconsistent. Trained musicians show narrower audiovisual temporal integration windows and quicker segregation, whereas experienced wine tasters seem more influenced by a wine's color in their aroma and flavor judgments than novices are. We argue that the inconsistency arises from a conflation of two formally distinct quantities: the prior probability that concurrent signals arise from a common source, and the coupling between the values of signals that share one. We present a generative model in which both are free parameters, along with channel precision and a decision criterion, that contains causal-inference and coupling-prior models as special cases. The model shows that the correlation between the values of two signals across an environment reflects only the product of the two priors, so that a correlation-tracking learner acquires the coupling when the signals always share a source, whereas separating the two priors requires representing causal structure; that binary common-source reports confound the common-cause prior with the decision criterion; that the coupling trades off against the measurement noise of the influencing channel unless its precision is measured independently; and that the two priors leave distinct signatures in how cross-modal influence varies with disparity. When the source is fixed, as for the color and odor of a wine, tighter coupling alone produces the conjunction of greater displacement by color and better discrimination between wines reported for experienced tasters, which no change in odor precision can produce. Simulations of a test battery combining continuous estimates, common-source reports and discrimination thresholds show that the parameters can be recovered, that a within-subject dissociation can be detected with conventional sample sizes under illustrative effect sizes, and that recovery fails in certain cases. The account yields a rule classifying environments by their base rate of common causation and their coupling strength, and the same ambiguity attends claims about altered multisensory processing in autism and aging. We also show that the most cited demonstration of expert susceptibility to color contains no expertise manipulation, and suggest that apparent expert biases may reflectwind calibration to real-world statistics.

piezas.titulo: Parenting in the Shadow of Enduring Health Conditions: Experiences of Parenting, Participation and Support.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Parenting is a central occupation that may be disrupted by enduring health conditions, yet how parents experience the interaction between health, parenting demands and support systems remains underexplored. This study explored parents' experiences living with an enduring health condition, focusing on participation, support needs and service access. Qualitative data were drawn from open-ended questions within a national cross-sectional e-survey of parents with enduring health conditions in Ireland. Responses from 218 participants were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Four themes were identified: impact on parenting roles, centrality of informal support networks, engagement with formal services and future service design. Parenting participation was influenced by fluctuating symptoms, environmental barriers and social expectations. Informal supports enabled participation but were often inconsistent, while formal services were frequently fragmented and difficult to access. Parenting is shaped by interacting health, environmental and systemic factors, highlighting the need for strengths-based, family-centred occupational therapy approaches.

piezas.titulo: Validity and Reliability of the Activity Card Sort 3 in Persons With Thumb Carpometacarpal Osteoarthritis.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceAlthough individuals with thumb carpometacarpal (CMC1) osteoarthritis (OA) commonly experience participation restrictions, participation-focused outcome measures remain underinvestigated, and clinicians primarily rely on assessments of impairments in body structures and functions.ObjectiveTo determine the concurrent validity, test-retest reliability, and precision of the Activity Card Sort 3 (ACS3) in individuals with nonoperative CMC1 OA.DesignSingle-cohort observational psychometric study with repeated measures over a 2-week interval.SettingRemote assessments conducted via videoconferencing.ParticipantsThirty-three adults with radiographically confirmed CMC1 OA completed two virtual assessments approximately 2 weeks apart.Outcomes and MeasuresConcurrent validity was examined by comparing ACS3 domain and total scores with the World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0 (WHODAS 2.0). Test-retest reliability of the "current," "previous," and "% retained" activities scores was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC 3,1 ). Precision was assessed using the standard error of measurement and minimal detectable change.ResultsThe ACS3 demonstrated good concurrent validity through strong associations with conceptually related WHODAS 2.0 domains. "Current" and "% retained" scores demonstrated good-to-excellent test-retest reliability across all domains. "Current" scores consistently showed the highest reliability and precision. "Previous" scores demonstrated lower reliability and greater measurement error, suggesting recall bias. Carrying forward "previous" scores from session 1 to session 2 improved the reliability of "% retained" scores.Conclusions and RelevanceThe ACS3 is a valid and reliable measure of participation for individuals with nonoperative CMC1 OA. The "current" and "% retained" scores may support occupational therapy practitioners in conducting participation-focused assessment of persons with CMC1 OA.

piezas.titulo: El malestar psicológico a través del inglés y otros idiomas
piezas.resumenOriginal: El malestar psicológico a través del inglés y otros idiomas emcamara 29/10/2026 26/11/2026 Fecha y hora: 26/11/26, 5pm CET Ponentes : Anna-Maria Bucur, Dalle Molle Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Università della Svizzera italiana (Italia) Presentador: Paolo Rosso, Universidad Politécnica de Valencia (España). Resumen: La presentación analiza cómo el procesamiento del lenguaje natural puede respaldar la investigación psicológica analizando interacciones procedentes de redes sociales para comprender mejor el malestar psicológico. Mientras que el PLN resulta eficaz a la hora de identificar patrones lingüísticos, la psicología articula la investigación definiendo los conceptos clave, explicando su relevancia y aportando un marco para interpretar los hallazgos. La ponencia comienza con varios estudios de caso centrados en la supervivencia al cáncer, la identificación de problemas de salud mental en la población general y la exploración de momentos de felicidad en personas diagnosticadas con depresión, todos ellos a partir de datos en inglés. A continuación, aborda consideraciones transculturales al trabajar con datos en idiomas distintos del inglés y evalúa los modelos del lenguaje de gran tamaño (LLM) para este fin. La presentación subraya que un PLN fundamentado en la teoría puede desvelar trayectorias psicológicas y ofrecer perspectivas valiosas para las intervenciones terapéuticas. No obstante, también destaca cómo la falta de datos de calidad y de evaluaciones adecuadas plantea retos a la hora de desarrollar métodos aplicables a lenguas más allá del inglés. Reseña: Ana-Maria Bucur es investigadora postdoctoral en el Instituto Dalle Molle de Inteligencia Artificial (IDSIA), Università della Svizzera italiana, donde trabaja en el Laboratorio de Recuperación de Información del profesor Fabio Crestani. Realizó un doctorado en cotutela entre la Universitat Politècnica de València y la Universidad de Bucarest, bajo la dirección de los profesores Paolo Rosso y Liviu P. Dinu. Ana-Maria ha participado en colaboraciones interdisciplinares que abarcan tanto la psicología como las humanidades digitales. Su investigación se centra principalmente en el procesamiento del lenguaje natural (PLN) aplicado a la salud mental, investigando en especial cómo las personas expresan sus estados psicológicos a través del lenguaje y de qué manera los métodos computacionales pueden mejorar nuestra comprensión de la salud mental y respaldar el bienestar. Más recientemente, ha estado explorando cómo influye la cultura en las manifestaciones de los trastornos mentales y cómo desarrollar métodos computacionales con sensibilidad cultural para un cribado de salud mental más inclusivo. piezas.titulo: Factors influencing health beliefs regarding facial nerve rehabilitation training in patients with peripheral facial paralysis: a qualitative study
piezas.resumenOriginal: ObjectiveTo investigate the factors influencing health beliefs regarding facial nerve rehabilitation training in patients with peripheral facial paralysis (PFP), and to provide a reference for developing precise and individualized facial nerve rehabilitation training programs for this population.MethodsGuided by the Health Belief Model (HBM), this descriptive qualitative study employed purposive sampling to recruit 16 patients with PFP who had received facial nerve rehabilitation training in healthcare settings. Semi-structured interviews were conducted, and the data were analyzed using codebook thematic analysis.ResultsThrough data analysis, five overarching themes and 23 subthemes were identified: Perceived Threat of the Disease (appearance impairment, emotional distress, disease course concern, diminished role functioning, disease burden); Perceived Benefits of Health Behaviors (improvement of facial paralysis symptoms, emotional improvement, social participation, image enhancement, reduced disease burden); Perceived Barriers to Health Behaviors (memory difficulties, inconsistencies in guidance content and methods, emotional interference, time–space constraints, low perceived importance); Cues to Action (professional guidance, post-discharge referral services, family support, stage goal setting, health benefits, peer support); and Self-efficacy (perseverance, ability to regulate training intensity).DiscussionHealth beliefs regarding facial nerve rehabilitation training in patients with PFP are influenced by multiple interrelated factors. Healthcare providers should promptly identify and respond to perceived barriers to health behaviors, reinforce the perception of disease threat and benefits of health behaviors, and utilize cues to action and self-efficacy as key entry points for intervention. Tailored rehabilitation guidance and recommendations should be provided to enhance patients' adherence to facial nerve rehabilitation training and improve their quality of life.

piezas.titulo: Increased activity without changes in coupling between somata and apical dendrites during visual mismatches
piezas.resumenOriginal: Leading theories of cortical function posit that sensory processing involves a comparison between top-down predictions and bottom-up sensory data. Tests of these theories have been hampered by experimental challenges related to simultaneously recording top-down and bottom-up signals in response to sensory stimuli that either do or do not match internally-generated predictions. Here, we conduct dual-plane 2-photon calcium imaging near-simultaneously from distal apical dendrites and somata of pyramidal neurons in each of 4 different regions of mouse visual cortex while the mice are presented with visual sequences that can either match or mismatch previously habituated visual stimuli. Specifically, we examine the responses in the distal apical dendrites and cell bodies of pyramidal neurons while mice view either movie clips that reverse unexpectedly or Gabor patch sequences that have orientations that do not match habituated patterns. We find that in response to unexpected reversals in natural movies, both the apical dendrites and somata show increased activity that decreases over repeated exposures, consistent with a prediction error response. However, we do not find any clear evidence for increased activity in response to mismatches in Gabor sequences, beyond possible release from adaptation effects. We additionally use volumetric images to connect dendritic and somatic compartments and examine the coupling between connected dendrites and cell bodies in layer 5 pyramidal neurons. We do not find evidence for changes in coupling in response to mismatch stimuli, either for natural movies or Gabor sequences. Our results are consistent across four regions of visual cortex. We also observe that increased responses to reversals in natural movies are stronger in layer 2/3 than layer 5 pyramidal neurons. Altogether, these data suggest that visual cortex is sensitive to deviations from previously-experienced naturalistic inputs. Our data do not suggest that this mismatch sensitivity extends to artificial stimuli, nor do they support theories of prediction error causing changes in the coupling between apical dendrites and somata.

piezas.titulo: MOF-VERIFY: A Failure-Aware Agentic Harness for MOF Hypothesis Verification
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2610.03056v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as reasoning components in AI-driven materials Co-Scientists, yet the reliability of the resulting verification pipeline remains unclear. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) provide a particularly challenging setting because structures may appear under different identifiers, synthesis outcomes depend strongly on experimental conditions, evidence is distributed across heterogeneous sources, and some hypotheses require computation rather than literature alone. We introduce a diagnostic benchmark with four task families covering structural grounding, synthesis-condition verification, evidence-sufficiency verification, and MLIP-based computational verification. T-MOF-1-3 are evaluated under closed-book, retrieval-enabled, and oracle-evidence settings to localize failures in knowledge access, evidence acquisition, and reasoning, while T-MOF-4 separately evaluates computational verification. Guided by these diagnosed failure modes, we develop MOF-Verify, a failure-aware agentic harness that targets structural, literature, evidence-sufficiency, and computational bottlenecks before producing a final verdict. Across multiple backbone LLMs, MOF-Verify improves the reported average over direct inference and retrieval-based baselines on this benchmark, with gains concentrated in structural grounding and evidence sufficiency. Benchmark records and release-status documentation are available at https://github.com/IMMS-Ewha/MOF-Verify-Benchmark.

piezas.titulo: Cortical responses to lipread and text-based audiovisual stimuli in adults with and without dyslexia
piezas.resumenOriginal: Phonetic recalibration enables listeners to adjust their perception of ambiguous speech sounds based on visual contextual information. In line with a specific difficulty in forming letter-speech sound associations, adults with dyslexia have been found to show no text-based, but intact lipread-based, recalibration. The underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear however. This fMRI study examined cortical responses during text-based and lipread-based phonetic recalibration in 34 adults (18 with dyslexia, 16 typical readers). Participants were exposed to ambiguous speech sounds /a?a/ paired with disambiguating visual information (“aba”/“ada” text or lipread videos), followed by auditory-only categorization trials. Contrary to previous findings, both groups showed robust text-based and lipread-based behavioral recalibration effects, with no significant group differences between typical and dyslexic readers. Neuroimaging data did yield group differences in the underlying cortical activation. Most notably, dyslexic readers demonstrated increased bilateral fusiform activation compared to typical readers during exposure to lipread videos and ambiguous speech sounds, with left fusiform activation specifically correlating with increased phonological processing difficulties. Additionally, typical readers exhibited higher right frontal activation during text-based audiovisual stimuli. These findings suggest that while adults with dyslexia did not differ significantly from typical readers in behavioral recalibration effects, they employed different neural processing strategies. Unexpectedly, this was particularly the case for lipread audiovisual stimuli. The relatively increased fusiform and superior temporal activation to lipread audiovisual stimuli in dyslexic readers possibly relates to subtle difficulties in phonological processing of ambiguous speech signals.

piezas.resumenOriginal: Functional autonomy reflects adolescents' participation across daily occupations. This cross-sectional study examined associations between functional autonomy, executive functions, self-management, and social-emotional strengths in 88 typically developing adolescents within a strength-based, multidimensional framework. Participants completed the Participation Activities Rating for Teenagers (Take PART) and standardized self-report measures (Teenage Executive Functioning Inventory, Self-Control and Self-Management Scale, and Social Emotional Health Survey-Secondary). Regression analyses identified inhibition and engaged living as primary factors associated with overall autonomy ( R 2 = .25), with domain-specific contributions from working memory and emotional competence. Cluster analysis revealed two functional profiles reflecting higher (Cluster 1) and lower (Cluster 2) cognitive-regulatory-emotional profiles. Inhibition and engaged living showed the strongest associations with overall autonomy. Functional autonomy was associated with executive functions, self-management, and social-emotional strengths. These findings support a multidimensional understanding of functional autonomy during adolescence and may inform individualized occupational therapy assessment and intervention planning.

piezas.titulo: Peer Mentoring Benefits in Rehabilitation for Individuals With Spinal Cord Injury: A Systematic Review.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Importance The lived experiences of peer mentors with spinal cord injury (SCI) provide distinct value in the rehabilitation process and contribute to improved outcomes. When combined with traditional therapy, peer mentorship programs can enhance life satisfaction among individuals living with SCI. Objective To explore the impact that peer-led mentorship programs and interventions have on the rehabilitation outcomes for individuals with a spinal cord injury (SCI). Data sources PubMed, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, ERIC, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, MedNar, and OpenGrey were searched between 2014 and 2024. The Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool was adapted and used to assess risk of bias in the included studies. Study selection and data collection Inclusion criteria included individuals with SCI who participated in peer mentorship and reported outcomes on quality of life, well-being, independence, or activities of daily living (ADLs) or instrumental ADLs. Exclusion criteria included interventions conducted via telehealth or reported outcomes of social participation. Findings Five articles were analyzed for synthesis, which included individuals 18 yr and older with an SCI. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Findings may have limited generalizability across different settings and populations because of the small number of available studies and variability in study designs, interventions, and outcome measures. None of the articles reviewed included occupational therapists. Conclusions and relevance This review highlighted the benefits of peer mentorship in enhanced life satisfaction. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Future research should examine the benefits of incorporating peer-led intervention programs across the continuum of care, including occupational therapy, in enhancing best practices in SCI rehabilitation. Plain-Language Summary: Peer mentorship programs can help people with spinal cord injuries adjust to daily life by providing guidance, support, and encouragement that professionals without lived experience may not offer. This review found that peer mentoring can improve psychological well-being and health management and reduce unplanned hospital visits. Evidence is limited because of the small number of studies and variations in study design; however, the results suggest that meaningful benefits may be present. Further research is needed to determine the most effective way to implement peer mentorship across rehabilitation settings.

piezas.titulo: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum
piezas.resumenOriginal: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum STAR Admin Thu, 06/15/2017 - 14:07 STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) and T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades) are two Colorado nonprofits who have partnered to create a series of respite camps serving adolescents who have autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Developmental Pathways has awarded the organizations a $25,000 grant to fund three F.U.S.E. (Fostering Unlimited Success and Empowerment) camps through 2018. STAR Institute offers premier treatment for SPD and brings expertise in social skills while T.AC.T. teaches trade and life skills to individuals with ASD and SPD with an emphasis on fostering independence and personal growth. “This is a very rare and exciting way to see two nonprofits interact. Our partnership to create F.U.S.E. allows both of our organizations to combine expertise in a way that best serves these adolescents to find new interests and gain the soft skills to successfully participate in peer groups and future workplaces”, says Dick Layton, Director of STAR Institute for SPD. The respite camps will be week-long day camps that host six students per camp ages 12-15 who have autism spectrum disorder. The camps will teach pre-vocational and vocational skills in a supportive, social, and inclusionary environment. Each camp has a different project for participants including: building a non-motorized go-cart with a partner, building an instrument to play in a band, and crafting board games. “The intended focus of F.U.S.E. is not just about offering a respite program for families. By generating new experiences for these adolescents, we hope to foster new skills, new interests, develop social skills, and give them a sense of empowerment to participate in what hopefully becomes a new hobby or future career interest”, says Danny Combs co-founder and president of T.A.C.T. SPD is a neurological disorder that disrupts the way an individual processes and responds to sensations. The disorder can affect people in only one sense–for example, just touch or just sight or just movement–or in multiple senses. One person with SPD may over-respond to touch sensation and find clothing, physical contact, other tactile sensory input to be unbearable and/or they may respond to visual or auditory or another sensory input. Another person might under-respond and show little or no reaction to stimulation, even pain or extreme hot and cold or just may be slow to respond to sensation. SPD and ASD have a high co-morbidity rate, but are also found to be standalone disorders. ASD refers to conditions categorized by challenges with social skills, repetitive behaviors, speech and nonverbal communication, as well as by unique strengths and differences that can occur on a range from mild to severe. Individuals with ASD and SPD frequently struggle with interpersonal skills over their lifetime and are often underestimated, which can lead to specific difficulty in career and relationships. F.U.S.E. aims to give individuals the ability to ignite new interests and feel empowered in group collaboration, which can lead to greater success in career and relationships. About STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder: The STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder, a Colorado 501(c)(3), is the world leader in treatment, research, and education for Sensory Processing Disorder, a neurological condition that disrupts the daily lives of more than 4 million Americans. The STAR Institute is the premier treatment center for children, adults and families living with Sensory Processing Disorder, feeding disorders, and other sensory conditions associated with ADHD, autism, and other developmental disorders. Dr. Lucy Jane Miller, founder of STAR Institute, is widely recognized as the leader in Sensory Processing Disorder research worldwide. Our programs are designed to empower individuals and develop interests and skills for life. To learn more visit: https://tactkids.org or call 720-460-0897. piezas.titulo: WeightLoop: Weight-Space Programming with Experimental Feedback
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2611.07319v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weight-space programming (WSP) shows that language models can reason about and rewrite neural network weights; recursive self-improvement (RSI) motivates feedback-driven improvement. Models guiding experiments receive concrete feedback: completed assays reveal prediction errors and inform what to test next. We introduce WeightLoop, a framework that turns experimental feedback into persistent updates to deployed predictors. GPT-6 Astra inspects a task specification and the model implementation, then writes a bounded, reusable parameter-editing program. As new measurements arrive, the program identifies prediction discrepancies, validates candidate edits using observed outcomes, and writes the selected changes back to the original model. The editor remains fixed while the predictor evolves, enabling repeated updates without further LLM calls or gradient retraining while preserving the original inference interface. In offline replay, targeted edits improve mean ranking utility in seven of eight endpoint-budget settings (all eight versus random edits) and mean final discovery across three sequential tasks. WeightLoop connects WSP with an RSI-inspired improvement loop, making experimental evidence a direct driver of model change and subsequent decisions.

piezas.titulo: Rule-Guided and Trajectory-Aware Repair for LLM-Based HLS Generation
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2611.07324v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising path for directly generating functionally correct and synthesizable HLS-C from natural-language specifications. However, existing approaches often struggle to turn multi-round tool feedback and reusable HLS knowledge into effective revisions, limiting end-to-end generation success. We propose MementoHLS, an agentic HLS generation framework built around executable and falsifiable dual-memory-guided repair. MementoHLS combines an Executable Repair Contract Library (ERCL), which converts cross-task HLS knowledge into evidence-gated repair actions, with a Reviewer-Grounded Falsification Ledger (RFL), which converts task-local repair history into trajectory evidence to suppress ineffective routes and preserve validated progress. To ensure reliable outcome attribution, a Same-Candidate Reviewer binds Parse, Compile, Testbench (TB), and Synthesis (Synth) outcomes to the corresponding candidate, while a Single-Commit Arbiter commits at most one candidate per round. Evaluated on 94 HLS-Eval and 170 Bench4HLS tasks, MementoHLS improves same-candidate TB$\wedge$Synth pass@1/pass@5 from 41.7%/57.4% to 58.9%/68.1% on HLS-Eval, and from 15.5%/32.9% to 32.4%/50.6% on Bench4HLS, demonstrating substantial improvements in end-to-end HLS generation reliability.

This is the first of a two-part series exploring how Google Cloud is bringing the foundational values of a high-performance parallel filesystem–TB/s throughput, sub-ms latency at high client scale, and POSIX support–to a broader set of use cases and users. Historically, due to the cost and special purpose nature of parallel filesystems, colder data had to be stored outside of the filesystem and AI developers have had to maintain separate, slower environments for writing code, compiling libraries, and managing repositories. This fragmentation increases the toil of manual data staging, dataset copying, and managing disjointed namespaces. Google Cloud Managed Lustre is solving these problems through our 6 cents/GB*month Dynamic Tier and by optimizing Managed Lustre performance for a range of development tasks and workloads – making Managed Lustre a “One-Stop Shop” for high-performance AI and HPC workloads. Lower Cost: More Lustre for Less with the Dynamic Tier The Managed Lustre Dynamic Tier provides sub-ms latency for hot data, which allows you to store all of your data in a single namespace, and costs only 6 cents/GB*month . Throughput, capacity scale and client scale: Throughput scales linearly with capacity up to 80 PB, while sub-ms latency for hot data remains stable as you scale to tens of thousands of clients. Single-flat fee: Predictable pricing. No independent charges for disk media types, data movement within the namespace, or metadata IOPS. Read Latencies: Sub-ms latencies for High-Performance Cache (SSD). The Capacity Pool (“HDD”) is built on Google Cloud Hyperdisk throughput, which has an average read latency of 10 to 30 ms . Recommended workloads for Dynamic Tier Multi-Epoch Training and/or Training with Optimized Fetch Sizes: Hot data is promoted to the High Performance Cache (SSD) after the first run. Larger data prefetch will allow you to take advantage of the Dynamic Tier cost structure and gain from low-latency SSD. Write-Heavy Checkpointing: Bursty checkpoint writes land directly in the High Performance Cache. Older checkpoints are transparently demoted to the Capacity Pool (HDD). Rapid Checkpoint Restore: New checkpoints are written to the High Performance Cache, enabling low-latency checkpoint restores. Interactive Snappiness for Developers: Low-latency tasks like git cloning, compiling libraries, or running notebooks benefit from a local-disk feel (~300µs average read latencies) on the same shared workspace hosting large training sets. Frictionless development: Lustre as a one-stop shop for developer’s workloads In addition to Managed Lustre’s scalability for large AI and HPC workloads (checkpoint/restart/data-loading), it also meets the demands for interactive work, meaning developers can start on Managed Lustre and stay on Managed Lustre throughout the entire workload lifecycle: Unified Foundation & Interactive Performance Consolidates the AI and HPC lifecycle into a single namespace, providing a "local disk" feel for interactive work (Read more about the latency benefits of Managed Lustre experienced by Salesforce and others ).
